newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghanistan's Taleban faced with fear and loathing.
newsitem.headline: Afghanistan's Taleban faced with fear and loathing.

text.p: Afghanistan's new Taleban rulers, besieged with blistering condemnation by human rights officials, also faced a grim military standoff on Thursday with troops loyal to the former government.

The hardline Taleban militia, who swept virtually unopposed into Kabul last Friday, shocked the world with their brutal execution of former president Najibullah and three aides followed by a series of harsh Islamic edicts.
Instead of international recognition, the Taleban have been greeted with suspicion -- and fear.

Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) leaders plan to meet in the Kazakh capital Almaty this weekend to discuss the fighting in Afghanistan as concern grows over a possible threat to southern border areas.

The CIS is especially concerned about Tajikistan's 1,500-km (900-mile) frontier with Afghanistan, patrolled by Russian-led border guards. The border has become an effective front line in the prolonged conflict between the pro-Moscow Tajik government in Dushanbe and Islamic guerrillas based in Afghanistan.
The Taleban, which in the Pashtu language means "seekers" or "students", was founded just two years ago by former guerrillas hardened by years of fighting with Soviet occupation troops.
It has said it would impose strict fundamentalist limits on women -- making them stop working, stay at home and wear veils in public. Men would have to wear beards.
Amnesty International said Taleban had taken up to 1,000 prisoners during house-to-house searches in Kabul.
It said it feared that civilians suspected of being sympathisers of ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani could be tortured or killed.

"Despite statements from their leadership suggesting moderation, it is clear that Taleban guards are busily implementing a reign of terror in Kabul," the human rights organisation said in a statement in London.
"Families are afraid to go out into the streets, afraid to answer their doors and afraid that their loved ones will suffer the brutal consequence of being found "un-Islamic' by the militia."
Amnesty said that children and women were being ill-treated by militia guards. In some areas girls' schools have been closed and women have not been allowed to leave their homes.
In Brussels, Europe's Commissioner for humanitarian aid Emma Bonino urged the European Union to be more vocal over the human rights situation in Afghanistan.
Bonino said the world had been surprisingly quiet over the fate of Afghanistan's people, especially minorities and women.
"The silence of the international community worries me... The reaction of the U.S. has been surprisingly mild," she said.
EU foreign ministers made no statement on Afghanistan when they met in Luxembourg on Tuesday.
The Taleban promise to govern Afghanistan according to Islamic Sharia law, including punishments such as death for murder, stoning for adultery and amputation for theft.

Militarily the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban, who control three-quarters of the country, were tiptoeing towards a battle with former government military chief Ahmed Shah Masood's Tajik fighters in his Panjsher Valley redoubt.
Masood has declared a state of emergency in the strategic valley and ordered an evacuation in anticipation of an attack.
The Taleban have bottled up the valley after sweeping north from Kabul over the past few days, capturing Golbahar town 10 km (six miles) away.

They appeared to be succeeding in their attempt to prevent a battle with the powerful warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who has marshalled a formidable force of tanks, guns and missiles at a vital tunnel northwest of the capital.

Colonel-General Chary, commander of Dostum's Jumbish-i-Milli frontline position, told reporters on Wednesday in what sounded like a warning to the Taleban forces: "We don't want to fight but we will defend our territory."
He had well-armed positions, including multiple-launch Grad missiles, tanks and heavy artillery, at both ends of the strategically vital tunnel, around 70 km (45 miles) from Kabul.

Russia's national security supremo, Alexander Lebed, suggested on Tuesday that Russia and other ex-Soviet republics might provide "material and moral" support to Dostum, Masood and Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar.
Lebed said the triumph of the Taleban was fraught with danger for Moscow and its CIS partners.
